questions.question: What should you have before testing a website you do not own?
options: Explicit permission and an agreed scope
questions.explanation: A public URL is not permission. Agree on authorization and scope before testing.

questions.question: Where should an application enforce access to protected data?
options: On the server for each protected operation
questions.explanation: The browser is controlled by the user. Server-side checks must protect each operation.

questions.question: Which boundary deserves security checks?
options: The boundary between untrusted input and trusted processing
questions.explanation: Treat incoming requests as untrusted and validate them before relying on their contents.

questions.question: What is the purpose of this practice self-check?
options: To help you review concepts locally
questions.explanation: This is a browser-local learning aid, not a secure examination or professional credential.

questions.question: What starts a typical HTTP exchange?
options: A browser or other client sends a request
The server reads the user’s mind
A CSS file creates an account
questions.explanation: The client sends a request, and the server sends a response.

questions.question: What does an HTTP status code describe?
options: The outcome of handling a request
questions.explanation: Status codes communicate outcomes such as success, redirect, client error or server error.

questions.question: Should a server trust a hidden form field just because it is hidden?
options: No, the client can modify it
questions.explanation: Hidden fields are still client-controlled input and require server-side validation.

questions.question: What does HTTPS protect in transit?
options: A user from every phishing page
The confidentiality and integrity of the connection
questions.explanation: TLS protects transport. Application authorization and trustworthy endpoints remain necessary.

questions.question: What is authentication?
options: Checking which resources someone may use
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines allowed actions.

questions.question: Why should a session identifier be difficult to guess?
options: So attackers cannot readily impersonate another session
questions.explanation: A valid session token can act as a credential, so it must be unpredictable and protected.

questions.question: What does HttpOnly do for a cookie?
options: Prevents page JavaScript from directly reading it
questions.explanation: HttpOnly restricts JavaScript access to the cookie; it is one defense, not a complete security guarantee.

questions.question: What should logout do to an active server session?
questions.explanation: A logout flow should end the session, not merely hide its interface.

questions.question: Which question does authorization answer?
options: Is this actor allowed to perform this action on this resource?
questions.explanation: Authorization checks the actor, operation and resource together.

questions.question: A request includes someone else’s record ID. What should the server do?
options: Check that the requesting actor is allowed to access that record
Skip checks if the URL is public
questions.explanation: Object-level permissions must be verified even when a valid record identifier is supplied.

questions.question: Is hiding an admin button sufficient access control?
options: Yes, if the label says private
No, enforce permission checks on the server
questions.explanation: Users can issue requests independently of visible buttons.

questions.question: What is a safe default when permission has not been granted?
questions.explanation: Deny by default and explicitly grant the required permission.

questions.question: Why do parameterized queries (prepared statements) prevent SQL injection?
options: They encrypt the entire database on disk
They compile the SQL command structure separately from the bound data parameters
They hide the URL bar in the browser
questions.explanation: Prepared statements separate the query structure from user data so bound values are never parsed as SQL commands.

questions.question: When can an application using an ORM still be vulnerable to SQL injection?
options: When it concatenates untrusted strings into raw SQL helpers or dynamic ORDER BY clauses
When database tables have primary keys
questions.explanation: Bypassing parameter binding with string interpolation or unvalidated dynamic identifiers reintroduces SQL injection.

questions.question: How should a dynamic sort column name (such as ?sort=created_at) be handled safely?
options: Concatenate it directly into ORDER BY
Match it against a strict server-side allowlist of permitted column names
Trust it if it comes from a dropdown menu
questions.explanation: Identifiers like column or table names cannot use standard value bind parameters, so they must be mapped through a strict allowlist.

questions.question: Why should raw database syntax errors be hidden from public HTTP responses?
options: They make CSS files load slower
They reveal query structure, table names, and database types that help attackers craft payloads
questions.explanation: Detailed database errors leak internal schema and query details; log them server-side and return generic error messages.

questions.question: Why must output encoding match the specific HTML context where data is placed?
options: Because HTML body text, attributes, URLs, and script blocks have different parsing rules in the browser
Because browsers only parse one tag per page
questions.explanation: Each context (HTML text, attribute, href/src URL, script) interprets different characters as control syntax.

questions.question: Why does HTML entity encoding alone not make href="{{userUrl}}" safe?
options: A javascript: URL scheme contains no angle brackets or quotes yet still executes code when clicked
Entity encoding only works in CSS
questions.explanation: URL attributes must also be scheme-validated so only safe protocols like https: or http: are allowed.

questions.question: What protection does the HttpOnly cookie attribute provide during an XSS incident?
options: It preventsCross-Site Scripting from happening at all
It stops injected JavaScript from reading the raw cookie value via document.cookie
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, reducing direct token theft, though injected scripts can still send authenticated requests.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a Content Security Policy (CSP) against XSS?
options: A defense-in-depth browser policy that restricts inline scripts and untrusted script sources
questions.explanation: CSP acts as a second line of defense that restricts where scripts can load and execute even if an encoding bug slips through.

questions.question: Which DOM property safely inserts untrusted text without parsing HTML tags?
questions.explanation: textContent inserts a literal text node, so characters like < and > are never parsed as HTML elements.

questions.question: In DOM-based XSS, what are "sources" and "sinks"?
options: Untrusted client-side inputs (like location.search) and dangerous DOM APIs (like innerHTML) that interpret markup or code
questions.explanation: A DOM vulnerability arises when data flows from an attacker-controllable source into an execution or rendering sink without sanitization.

questions.question: What check is essential inside a window postMessage event listener?
options: Verifying event.origin against an explicit list of trusted origins and validating message structure
Checking whether dark mode is enabled
Reloading the page before reading event.data
questions.explanation: Any window can call postMessage, so listeners must verify event.origin before trusting event.data.

questions.question: How should an application render user-authored Markdown or rich HTML safely?
options: Pass the rendered HTML through a strict allowlist sanitizer before inserting it into the DOM
Strip only <script> tags using a single regular expression
questions.explanation: Regex blacklists miss event handlers like onerror/onload; a parser-backed allowlist sanitizer is required.

questions.question: Why can a cross-site page trigger a CSRF attack when a user is signed in?
options: Because browsers automatically attach ambient cookies for the target origin unless restricted
Because the attacker can read the user’s password from localStorage across origins
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the fact that browsers include destination-origin cookies automatically on cross-site requests.

questions.question: Why shouldn’t GET requests ever be used to change server state (such as deleting an item)?
options: Normal link clicks, image tags, prefetchers, and SameSite=Lax top-level navigations can trigger GET requests with cookies attached
GET requests are slower than POST requests
Browsers block GET requests on mobile
questions.explanation: GET must be safe and idempotent; state changes belong on POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE protected by anti-CSRF controls.

questions.question: Why can’t a malicious third-party website simply read a page’s anti-CSRF token and include it?
options: Because the Same-Origin Policy blocks cross-origin scripts from reading responses from the target origin
Because anti-CSRF tokens are stored only on paper
Because browsers block forms on third-party sites
questions.explanation: While a cross-origin site can submit a form, the Same-Origin Policy prevents it from reading the target site’s response to discover the token.

questions.question: What does setting SameSite=Lax on a session cookie do?
options: It sends the cookie on every cross-site iframe and fetch request
It withholds the cookie on cross-site subrequests (such as background POST forms or images) while sending it on top-level safe navigations
It deletes the cookie after 60 seconds
It makes the cookie readable by third-party domains
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax blocks cookies on cross-site subrequests and POSTs while preserving normal link navigation into the site.

questions.question: What makes Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) dangerous in cloud and internal networks?
options: It changes the user’s browser font
It slows down client-side CSS animations
The outbound request originates from the trusted server, which may have access to loopback services, private networks, or cloud metadata IPs
questions.explanation: SSRF lets an external caller pivot through the server’s network position to reach internal-only endpoints.

questions.question: Why is validating a URL string before calling fetch() often insufficient to stop SSRF?
options: Because an allowed external domain can return an HTTP 302 redirect or DNS record pointing to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254
Because HTTPS URLs cannot be parsed
Because fetch() only works in browsers
questions.explanation: Redirects and DNS resolution happen after string parsing, so the resolved IP and redirect behavior must also be controlled.

questions.question: Which IP address is commonly targeted in cloud SSRF attacks to reach instance metadata?
questions.explanation: Cloud providers commonly expose instance metadata on the link-local address 169.254.169.254.

questions.question: Which combination best defends a feature that must fetch remote webhooks?
options: Trusting any URL that starts with https://
Blocking private/loopback IP ranges after DNS resolution, disabling redirects, and routing outbound traffic through an isolated egress network
Hiding the webhook input field in CSS
questions.explanation: Defense in depth combines connection-time IP validation, disabled redirects, and network-level egress isolation.

questions.question: Why shouldn’t a server rely solely on the multipart Content-Type header to validate an upload?
options: Because Content-Type is only sent over HTTP/1.0
Because the client controls the Content-Type header and can label any payload as image/png
Because Content-Type is stripped by TLS
questions.explanation: Multipart headers and filenames are user-controlled input and can be trivially forged in an HTTP request.

questions.question: Why can allowing users to upload SVG images served from the main site origin cause Stored XSS?
options: SVG files are larger than PNG files
SVG is an XML document format that can contain executable <script> tags and event handlers when viewed directly in a browser
questions.explanation: When a browser navigates directly to an SVG on the application origin, embedded scripts execute in that origin.

questions.question: How should uploaded filenames be stored on disk or in object storage?
options: Use the exact filename provided by the user
Generate a new random server-side identifier (such as a UUID) with a strictly allowlisted extension
Prepend the user’s password to the filename
Store all files in the public JavaScript folder
questions.explanation: Server-generated random keys prevent path traversal, overwrites, and dangerous double extensions.

questions.question: Which response headers help prevent browsers from executing user-downloaded files as active HTML?
questions.explanation: nosniff prevents MIME-type sniffing and Content-Disposition: attachment prompts download rather than inline execution.

questions.question: Which CORS configuration is dangerously insecure for authenticated endpoints?
options: Not sending CORS headers at all
Allowing only a single exact trusted origin
Reflecting any arbitrary request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
questions.explanation: Reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials enabled lets any malicious website read authenticated responses.

questions.question: What attack do CSP frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options prevent?
options: Clickjacking (redressing a sensitive page inside a transparent or disguised iframe)
questions.explanation: Framing restrictions prevent untrusted origins from embedding your application inside an iframe.

questions.question: What does Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) instruct the browser to do?
options: Send all cookies to third-party domains
Automatically use HTTPS for future requests to the domain and refuse insecure HTTP connections
questions.explanation: HSTS protects users against SSL-stripping and accidental cleartext HTTP requests.

questions.question: What is the purpose of X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff?
options: To stop browsers from guessing a response’s MIME type and executing non-script files as HTML or JavaScript
questions.explanation: nosniff forces the browser to honor the declared Content-Type header instead of sniffing executable content.

questions.question: Why is rate limiting by IP address alone often not enough to stop login or OTP brute-forcing?
options: IP addresses cannot be read by web servers
IP rate limiting only works on UDP
Browsers hide IP addresses over HTTPS
Attackers can distribute attempts across thousands of rotating proxy IPs while targeting a single victim account
questions.explanation: Effective protection combines per-IP limits with per-account attempt budgets and backoff.

questions.question: Which items must NEVER be written into application or security logs?
options: Plaintext passwords, active session cookies, bearer tokens, and secret API keys
The request path and HTTP method
questions.explanation: Secrets in logs turn log viewers and backups into credential leaks; always redact sensitive headers and fields.

questions.question: How should a 6-digit MFA or password-reset code endpoint be protected?
options: Allow unlimited attempts as long as the code expires in 24 hours
Put the code in the page title
Enforce a strict per-code attempt limit (such as 5 tries), short expiration, and immediate invalidation after use
Validate the code only in client-side JavaScript
questions.explanation: A 6-digit code has only 1,000,000 possibilities and can be guessed quickly without strict attempt caps and short TTLs.

questions.question: Why should authorization boundaries be covered by automated CI regression tests?
options: So developers don’t need server-side checks
So a refactor that accidentally drops a permission check fails the build before reaching production
To make the HTML file smaller
questions.explanation: Automated negative tests (asserting 401/403 for unauthorized callers) catch access-control regressions early.

questions.question: Which of these is a vulnerability rather than a threat?
options: A supplier whose account was breached last month
One shared password used by all four staff
questions.explanation: A threat is whatever could cause the loss; a vulnerability is the gap that lets it succeed. You cannot remove a thief, but you can stop sharing one password.

questions.question: You have just installed a control. What is the last step of the loop?
options: Buy a second control in case the first fails
Write a policy about the control
Check that the control still works
Tell the team it is done
questions.explanation: Verification is the step everyone skips and the only one that catches a control that quietly stopped working.

questions.question: When does an ordinary software bug become a security issue?
options: When it crosses a boundary someone was supposed to control
When it is hard to fix
questions.explanation: Lots of bugs are just bugs. They become security-relevant when they let somebody past a boundary — reading data they should not, or acting as somebody else.

questions.question: Which is the better first question to ask about a system you are protecting?
options: What would we hate to lose, and would we notice it going?
What did the last security product advertise?
questions.explanation: Start from the asset and from how you would find out it was gone. Tools come last, and usually turn out to be cheaper than expected.

questions.question: A printed salary sheet is left on the office printer. Which is true?
options: Information security problem, with no cyber element
Neither — it is an HR problem
questions.explanation: Nothing digital leaked and no system was touched. Information security covers information wherever it lives, including paper.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
Every cyber security problem is also an information security problem, but not the reverse
Every information security problem is also a cyber problem
Cyber security is a subset of nothing
questions.explanation: Computers hold information, so a cyber problem is always an information problem. Information on paper or in a conversation has no cyber element at all.

questions.question: The same employee file sits on a shared drive readable by everyone in the company. Which applies?
options: Both: the rule about who may read it, and the permissions that enforce it
Neither, if the file is not secret
questions.explanation: The policy is information security; the permissions that actually enforce it are cyber security. That is why the two are usually handled together.

questions.question: What do most real incidents start with?
options: A nation-state actor with a zero-day
Information crossing a boundary nobody was watching
questions.explanation: Boring boundary failures — an attachment to a personal address, a link shared too widely — explain far more incidents than clever attacks do.

questions.question: A transfer posts twice and your balance shows the wrong number. Which goal failed?
options: None — it is a display bug
questions.explanation: Everything is reachable and nothing leaked; the value itself is wrong. That is integrity.

questions.question: Which goal's failures usually go unnoticed the longest?
questions.explanation: An outage is obvious and a wrong balance is visible. Somebody else reading your data looks exactly like nothing happening, which is why it can run for months.

questions.question: Keeping more backups improves availability but makes which goal harder?
questions.explanation: Every extra copy is another place the data can leak from. Adding a control almost always costs something somewhere else.

questions.question: What is the right way to handle the tension between the three goals?
options: Pick one goal and ignore the other two
Decide deliberately which one you would sacrifice first, and write it down
questions.explanation: The point is not to win the trade-off, it is to make it on purpose instead of discovering it during an incident.

questions.question: A cable lock that can be cut in nine seconds is which of the four?
questions.explanation: It is the specific gap that lets the loss happen. The thief is the threat; the bicycle is the asset.

questions.question: Which one is a threat and not a vulnerability?
options: A shared password used by four staff
A server that has not been patched since last year
questions.explanation: You cannot remove a thief from the world. You can close the gaps that make theft easy, which is why the other three are the ones you fix.

questions.question: Bots replay leaked passwords against a login page with no rate limit. What do you fix?
options: The vulnerability: add a rate limit and require a second factor
Nothing — the passwords were leaked elsewhere
The risk, by renaming the login page
questions.explanation: You cannot stop bots existing. You can make a leaked password insufficient, which turns a cheap automated attack into an expensive manual one.

questions.question: Risk is best described as which of these?
options: How likely the loss is, combined with how much it would hurt
questions.explanation: Every system carries some risk. The useful question is whether it is understood and priced, not whether it exists.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: The attack surface is the one route that was used; the vector is the total set
The attack surface is the total set of ways in; a vector is the one that was used
They are two words for the same thing
The surface only counts things you built recently
questions.explanation: You count and reduce the surface. You read about a vector afterwards, in the incident report.

questions.question: Which entry point is most often forgotten?
options: A staging copy from last year, still online, with the default password
questions.explanation: The forgotten entries are usually weaker than the ones you are carefully testing, because nobody has looked at them since the day they were set up.

questions.question: You ship a new feature. What should you ask before asking whether it works?
options: How many users will use it?
Does it look good on mobile?
questions.explanation: Every entry point is a promise to authenticate, validate, log and patch. Best to know what you promised before you find out the hard way.

questions.question: Every entry point you add is a promise to do which four things?
questions.explanation: Those four are the ongoing cost of exposing something. A form you never patch is a form that gets used against you.

questions.question: A backup that has never been restored is best described as…
options: Unnecessary if the disk is new
questions.explanation: The test is the control. Until you have restored from it, you do not know that it works — you know that it ran.

questions.question: A company has three prevention products and nothing that detects or recovers. What is wrong?
options: They covered one stage three times and left the other two empty
They need a fourth prevention product
questions.explanation: When prevention fails — and it eventually does — nothing tells you, and nothing helps you recover. Coverage across stages beats depth in one.

questions.question: A door code on the server room is which kind of control?
questions.explanation: It is a thing in the world (physical), and it stops the event rather than reporting it (preventive).

questions.question: Which set covers all three stages for a stolen laptop?
options: Two antivirus products and a firewall
A policy that laptops must not be left unattended
Full-disk encryption; a sign-in alert; remote wipe and a tested backup
questions.explanation: Prevent, detect, correct — one control at each stage. The policy from the third option is useful too, but it covers one stage only.

questions.question: Why does least privilege exist?
options: Because access only ever accumulates: nobody asks for less
Because it removes the need for passwords
questions.explanation: People ask for access to do a job and never ask to have it removed afterwards. That is why the permissions you have today are never the permissions you granted.

questions.question: Four people share one admin account with the password on a note. What is the first fix?
options: Give each person their own account
questions.explanation: Until each person has their own account you cannot tell who did what, or revoke one person without locking out the rest. Everything else can wait.

questions.question: Automated attacks scan everything and take whatever is open. What follows?
options: A small organisation is not a target, so it can wait
Being small means you are not attacked deliberately — which is not the same as being safe
Automated attacks are easy to spot
questions.explanation: You are probably not chosen. You may still be swept up, because scanning costs the attacker almost nothing.

questions.question: A policy says only two people have admin access. Which habit makes sure that is true?
questions.explanation: Rules drift away from reality. Only checking the actual permissions tells you what is really granted, as opposed to what was decided once.
